facts.t: Appears in 6.43% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (1,528 paintings, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 990).
In our 23,781-painting archive it is more common than 90% of the named colors.
Peaks in the 1200s: found in 8.5% of the 142 paintings we have from then (12 paintings). Against the same museums' baseline that is 1.8x the expected rate.
Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color (37% of the 990 paintings, by lightness rank within each painting, so varnish cannot fake it).
Painted most often by John Singer Sargent (21 of 287 works here, 7% of them). No painter stands out against the museum baseline.

First seen in our archive in 1000 (cma-133068); the third-earliest painting is 1000, and the latest 1943 (1272 dated paintings, at least 2% of the canvas, as photographed). The archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first. That is 650 years before the name's earliest record in our sources (1650): the match is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of the pigment or dye.
Most over-represented in Nepal (4.0x expected; 6 of 25 paintings).
Shares canvases with Veinous Blood Red and Fontainebleau more than chance (lift 6.3 and 5.7; n=115 and 76).
In printed English the word peaks in the 1880s and rose fastest in the 1880s (Google Books, adjective use only, which is the color sense).
